name: 手打蕎麦 ふじや (Teuchi Soba Fujiya)

claims.text: The restaurant's menu structure offers a 100% buckwheat (juwari) noodle alongside its standard wheat-blended (nihachi) noodle, but no dedicated gluten-free prep area, fryer, or cooking water is documented, and tempura is wheat-battered.

汁は良質な本節からとった出汁とかえしを合わせています (The tsuyu combines dashi taken from quality honbushi/dried bonito with kaeshi) — confirms both a non-vegan bonito dashi AND a wheat-soy-sauce kaeshi in the sauce served with all noodles, including juwari.
claims.source: https://soba-fujiya.jp/ (shop's own description, quoted in web search snippets)

claims.text: ベースの蕎麦は二八そばですが、十割そばに変更することも可能です (The base soba is nihachi/80-20 wheat blend, but it can be changed to juwari) — the default product contains wheat; juwari is only an upgrade swap made in the same hand-cutting operation.

Restaurant offers hand-made 100% buckwheat soba AND crispy wheat-battered tempura in the same small shop; multiple listings describe no gluten-free menu, no dedicated fryer, and no allergen-handling information.

General guidance: 'many dried and fresh versions of soba noodles in Japan are nonetheless mixed with wheat' and soba shops routinely use wheat-soy tsuyu and shared boiling water — celiacs are advised to confirm directly; no source documents Fujiya doing any of this safely.
A wheat-free (100% buckwheat) noodle option is a standing menu item rather than a special request, which is a meaningful GF-aware baseline compared to shops offering only wheat-blended soba.

name: TEXMEX FACTORY 渋谷公園通り店（テクスメクスファクトリー） (TEXMEX FACTORY Shibuya Koendori)

claims.text: The restaurant serves both corn and wheat 'flower' tortillas side by side as part of an all-you-can-eat buffet-style taco service, with no mention anywhere of separate gluten-free prep, utensils, or stations.
Corn tortillas (naturally gluten-free) are offered as an alternative to wheat 'flower' tortillas across the taco menu.
A plant-based 'Veggie Meat' taco/lunch option is listed alongside the meat-based tacos, giving vegetarians a menu item that doesn't require special requests.

name: タイガーデン 渋谷店 (Thai Garden Shibuya)

claims.text: The restaurant accommodates requests to adjust spice level and vegetarian dietary requests, per multiple listing-site descriptions of the restaurant's service.
Kitchen staff trained in Thailand and the restaurant holds Thai Select government certification for authentic Thai cuisine, suggesting attentiveness to traditional recipe composition.

name: 豆腐料理 空野 渋谷 (Tofu Ryori Sorano Shibuya)

claims.text: A 'wheat gluten skewers' dish (made from fu, i.e. wheat gluten) is offered as a vegan-friendly menu item — it is plant-based but contains gluten, so it is not a safe option for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners despite appearing on 'vegan' recommendation lists.
Fresh tofu-skin sashimi is served with standard soy sauce (shoyu), wasabi, and sudachi — no tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative was mentioned.

A reviewer asked staff whether a 'vegetarian'-marked menu item was vegan; staff initially said yes, but on double-checking it turned out the dish actually contained chicken — indicating menu dietary labels are not fully reliable and should be verbally reconfirmed per dish.

Reviewers describe a 'fantastic selection of vegan and vegetarian food' with staff willing to identify vegan-suitable dishes when asked, and an English menu that makes communicating dietary needs easier.
Core tofu dishes — cold silken tofu, fresh tofu-skin sashimi, and tofu gelato — are naturally vegan and were specifically praised by vegan diners on abillion.

name: 東京純豆腐 新宿店 (Tokyo Sundubu Shinjuku (Tokyo Jundoufu Shinj)

claims.text: The standard sundubu broth used chain-wide contains clams, fried tofu (abura-age), egg, and shellfish extract, and is prepared in a shared kitchen alongside meat and seafood dishes, so cross-contact with wheat/gluten-containing ingredients is likely.
Chain-wide allergen listings for the soup include wheat (小麦), soy, and sesame among the ingredients used in the gochujang-based broth.

All standard sundubu broths include clams, egg, and shellfish extract as base ingredients, so the shared broth is not suitable for vegan diners and cross-contact with animal products is inherent to the standard menu.

At least one Tokyo Sundubu branch (Ikebukuro) keeps a printed allergy/ingredient chart near the entrance/register that staff can check with guests on request; this practice is not separately confirmed for the Shinjuku branch.
Diners can customize spice level (1-6), soup type, and rice portion at order time, which gives some control over what goes into the bowl even though the base broth itself is fixed.

name: とんかつ ゆたか (Tonkatsu Yutaka)

claims.text: All cutlets are coated in house-made panko baked from domestic wheat bread, so the breading itself contains gluten; no gluten-free preparation is described by the restaurant or reviewers.
The menu centers entirely on pork cutlets and other meat/seafood dishes; no vegan or vegetarian dishes appear on the published menu.

The signature oyako-don is finished with the shop's original tare (simmering sauce); no gluten-free or wheat-free tare/soy sauce was mentioned in any source, and Japanese tare of this kind is typically soy-sauce based (soy sauce normally contains wheat).

The brand's signature broth/tare is described (for the technique used across its stores) as built on bonito, mackerel, and horse-mackerel dashi, meaning fish stock underlies core menu items such as the oyako-don.

name: 鶏そば・ラーメン Tonari (Torisoba Ramen Tonari)

claims.text: The tare is built from 'Shichifuku,' a certified organic white soy sauce (shiro shoyu) — a wheat-based product — with no gluten-free substitute mentioned in any source.
The house broths are chicken-bone based and finished with bonito (katsuo) dashi; no vegetable-only broth or plant-based bowl was identified.
The kitchen states it avoids chemical seasoning (no MSG), instead building umami from dried shiitake mushroom, dried shrimp, and slow-simmered chicken bones.
